scenarios.title: CHAIN found yesterday, locked today
scenarios.setup: A nightly order update reads a record successfully, but UPDATE now fails with a record-in-use message.
evidence: WRKOBJLCK shows another job holding the record.

steps.title: Separate lookup from update
steps.detail: Confirm the record was found, then identify the lock owner and whether the retry uses a fresh read.

steps.title: Inspect the competing job
steps.detail: Use the job log and lock details to determine whether the holder is active business work or a stale session.

steps.title: Choose a bounded retry
steps.detail: Re-read and retry only when the application contract permits it; otherwise record and route the conflict.

branches.condition: The holder is active user work
branches.action: Wait or notify the operator, then revalidate the record before updating.
branches.why: The lock may be protecting a legitimate change.

branches.condition: The holder is an ended or abandoned session
branches.action: Follow your operations policy to clean up the session and verify the lock is released.
branches.why: Ending work without evidence can lose user changes.

branches.condition: The record changed during the wait
branches.action: Reapply business validation against the new image or reject the stale request.
branches.why: A successful retry must not overwrite a newer decision.

verification: The job log records the chosen branch and final SQL/RPG status.
A concurrent test proves no stale record is overwritten.

quiz.question: What must follow a delayed UPDATE?
quiz.explanation: The record may have changed while locked.

scenarios.title: A nullable amount breaks a report
scenarios.setup: A report expects zero but receives a null indicator for an optional amount.
evidence: The report must distinguish unknown from zero.

steps.title: Inspect the declaration
steps.detail: Confirm the column nullability and the host variable indicator definition.

steps.title: Define business meaning
steps.detail: Decide whether NULL is shown as blank, labelled unknown, or intentionally mapped to zero.

steps.title: Test both states
steps.detail: Run a row with NULL and a row with a real zero, then compare output.

branches.action: Preserve the indicator and render an explicit not-supplied value.
branches.why: Zero would change the business meaning.

branches.condition: The report contract defines NULL as zero
branches.action: Use an explicit SQL expression or indicator-aware mapping.
branches.why: The conversion becomes documented and testable.

branches.action: Trace joins and expressions before changing the display.
branches.why: A join can introduce nulls even when a base column is required.

verification: NULL and zero produce distinct expected output when required.
The job log has no conversion or indicator error.

quiz.question: What distinguishes NULL from zero?
options: The null indicator and business contract
quiz.explanation: NULL is absence or unknown information.

scenarios.title: The batch job is waiting
scenarios.setup: A submitted job remains in MSGW and downstream work has not started.
evidence: The job log contains an inquiry message.
No application failure message has appeared.

steps.title: Read the inquiry
steps.detail: Identify the message, sender, and expected reply rather than ending the job immediately.

steps.title: Check the runbook
steps.detail: Match the inquiry to the approved operator response and business window.

steps.title: Verify continuation
steps.detail: After the reply, confirm the next program step and completion message.

branches.action: Use the approved reply and monitor the job.
branches.why: MSGW can be normal operator coordination.

branches.action: Preserve the job log and escalate before replying.
branches.why: A wrong reply can corrupt processing.

branches.action: Stop the loop and investigate the originating condition.
branches.why: Repeated retries hide the root cause.

verification: The job completes with its normal completion message.
The inquiry and response are recorded.

sources.title: IBM: Work with messages and message queues

quiz.question: What does MSGW tell you by itself?
options: Only that the job is waiting
quiz.explanation: Read the inquiry context before deciding.

scenarios.title: The new service program is not used
scenarios.setup: A replacement service program was deployed, but a long-running job still shows old behavior.
evidence: The new object has the expected export.
A fresh job sees the new behavior.

steps.title: Compare activation age
steps.detail: Establish whether the caller activation existed before the replacement.

steps.title: Inspect signatures
steps.detail: Confirm the export and binder language remain compatible.

steps.title: Plan lifecycle
steps.detail: Coordinate a controlled new activation or restart after preserving work.

branches.action: Create a controlled fresh activation and compare results.
branches.why: Existing activations can continue using their loaded copy.

branches.action: Rebuild dependent callers and follow the compatibility policy.
branches.why: A replacement cannot repair an incompatible contract.

branches.action: Inventory activation ages and roll the change gradually.
branches.why: Mixed versions need deliberate rollout evidence.

verification: A fresh job resolves the replacement export.
The deployment record names the affected activations and restart window.

quiz.question: Why can an old job keep old service-program behavior?
options: Its activation may already hold the old copy
quiz.explanation: Replacement and activation lifecycle are separate concerns.
